results.finding: sections, unit counts and unit forms match the spec

The cold outline lists the spec's controlling ideas in the spec's order across all 59 aligned units (p11 glossary before p10 three ways, p41 measures before p36 rule, p38 retired interface after p50), with only the three intro callouts unmatched; deterministic structure check also passes.
Same as reverse_outline_matches_spec: the outliner's summaries match sections[].paragraphs[] in order and content; no unit is missing, added or reordered.
The outliner marked no unit as holding two ideas; each draft paragraph carries the one idea its spec paragraph declares.

Every body paragraph ties to a supporting claim: scene to S2/S3, three ways to S1/S2, index section to S3/S4, runs-on-index to S5, reviews to S6, choices/stages/practice to S2/S4/S5, failures to S4-S6.

Each table and figure is introduced or followed by a sentence saying what it shows (e.g. 'The report made three things visible', 'The diagram shows the search service as a consumer of four systems of record', 'Behind the table is the pricing chapter's rule', 'The table's first two rows carry the difference between products'); quotations (Nigam et al., Elastic, Directive) are each followed by their consequence.

results.draft_locus: What Runs on the Index: Ranking, Recommendations and Wholesale Search ¶9
results.quote: Wholesale reuses this section's first decision, now for prices per account.
results.finding: The declared pickup is search for consumers and the in-index or query-time decision; the back-reference says 'this section's first decision', but this section's first part is relevance and rules, and the decision meant belongs to the previous section (The Index as a Copy). Both flow readers had to re-read to find it.

The introduction opens on the declared intriguing example (the waterproof jacket whose rating lives in a spreadsheet), bridges to the index as a copy owning none of its facts, and states thesis and roadmap; none of placeholder, restated question, dictionary, 'dawn of man' or book report.

'What to Take Away' opens on the chapter's opening jacket, not 'in conclusion'; it introduces no new subtopic, does not end on a restated thesis alone, and sorts the take-aways by how settled they are before the questions and hand-off.

p51a states what no single section does (the jacket, the stale 'in stock', the expired rule and the lost review are one fault, none owned by the search team) and gives the so-what: 'the first money goes to synonyms, product attributes and a stock feed, not to a search vendor', with the 9.4% to 4.1% illustration.

The conclusion returns to the waterproof jacket ('The chapter opened with a waterproof jacket that search could not find because its rating lived in a spreadsheet ... No ranking algorithm could have found the jacket; a synonym found most of what was lost, and from Q3 2027 the attribute finds the rest'), as callback.to declares.

The cold reader names a data gap first: the word or attribute is in nothing the index reads ('titled shell jacket', rating 'lives only in the seasonal spreadsheet', search indexes title, description, type and tags), a missing synonym, or an unindexed product; and checks the zero-result rate and top failing queries per language and which fields are indexed before any new engine. Matches expected.

The cold reader answers: only a coarse 'available' flag in the index, updated by stock events, with the exact answer from the availability service at query time, because an indexed fact is only as fresh as the last indexing run and stock changes by the second (the two-hour Phantom Stock). Matches expected.

The cold reader answers: how each review was collected and the order it is linked to, kept in the merchant's own store, because Directive (EU) 2019/2161 makes purchaser status material and blacklists claiming real purchasers without reasonable steps to check. Matches expected. (The reader noted the KEY POINTS attribute the provenance duty to 'EU and US rules' while the body gives only the EU duty; recorded under flow_is_followable.)

From the introduction alone the reader predicts, in order, the Kestrel & Pine search report, the vocabulary and three ways of finding, the index as a copy with its three conditions, what runs on it (ranking, filters, AI retrieval, wholesale), reviews, the product comparison and measures, the scale stages, vendor documentation, and the failures with detection and recovery; evidence predicted: the Kestrel & Pine case, vendor documentation, EU and US review rules, search metrics. Substance matches expected. Minor gaps: the reader could not name the three ways, did not foresee usability research (Baymard) or personalization, and unsure whether recommendations and merchandising are covered.
